candidates.title: Designing robot-to-robot interaction to support early-stage engagement in a teleoperated Robot Avatar system with multiple robots
candidates.abstract: Teleoperated Robot Avatars enable operators to provide customer service from remote locations. Effective persuasive interaction requires more than information presentation; customers' attention and engagement must be elicited before their attitudes and behavior can be influenced. Social presence may support this type of engagement. Based on prior research, we conceptualize a Robot Avatar's social presence as the extent to which customers perceive it, i.e., not as a machine or information medium, but as a social entity customers can attend to and interact with. Therefore, we examined a design approach intended to enhance a Robot Avatar's social presence by forming a social context around it. We developed GayaRobo, comprising one teleoperated Robot Avatar and two supporting Gaya robots. Rather than approaching users as independent agents, the Gaya robots respond to the Robot Avatar's utterances via speech and movement, thereby forming a social context centered on the avatar. We conducted a field experiment at a commercial complex in Osaka, Japan, to compare observable early-stage engagement behaviors of passersby toward the Robot Avatar across three experimental conditions. The same three-robot configuration was used under three conditions: the Gaya robots responded to the Robot Avatar, only the Robot Avatar spoke, or only the Gaya robots spoke. Two annotators coded four behaviors among 1,379 passersby in 270 min of video recordings: looking at the Robot Avatar, approaching it, talking to it, and picking up a flyer. After correction for multiple testing, only approaching the Robot Avatar was significantly associated with experimental condition and occurred more frequently than expected under the inter-robot interaction condition. These findings provide behavioral evidence that the inter-robot interaction condition was associated with approaching the Robot Avatar, an observable indicator of early-stage engagement. Because social presence was not directly measured, the findings did not demonstrate that GayaRobo enhanced the Robot Avatar's social presence. Nevertheless, they highlight approach behavior as a relevant observable outcome for future evaluations of designs that consider the social context surrounding a Robot Avatar in customer service settings.

candidates.title: A study on user continuance intention for children’s intelligent companion robots based on BERTopic-PLS-SEM-fsQCA
candidates.abstract: The children’s intelligent companion robot market faces the industry-wide challenge of “high initial adoption yet low sustained retention.” Existing research has predominantly relied on single-method approaches, leaving the psychological mechanisms and configurational pathways driving user continuance intention insufficiently understood. This study constructs a sequential multi-method research framework integrating “BERTopic thematic mining—PLS-SEM linear validation—fsQCA configurational analysis.” Drawing on 6,405 valid online reviews from JD.com and 440 valid questionnaire responses, the study adopts an integrated theoretical framework combining the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) and the Value-based Adoption Model (VAM). BERTopic thematic mining identified six core demand dimensions from consumer reviews: perceived usefulness, perceived enjoyment, visual aesthetics, social/gifting value, technical reliability, and expectation confirmation. PLS-SEM analysis reveals that satisfaction is the strongest predictor of continuance intention ( β = 0.705, p < 0.001), explaining 50.3% of its variance ( R ² = 0.503). Perceived value ( R ² = 0.571) is jointly driven by expectation confirmation ( β = 0.230), perceived usefulness ( β = 0.197), technical reliability ( β = 0.163), social/gifting value ( β = 0.141), visual aesthetics ( β = 0.106), and perceived enjoyment ( β = 0.104). Notably, perceived enjoyment exhibits a distinctive dual-pathway mechanism, influencing continuance intention both indirectly through perceived value and directly through satisfaction ( β = 0.232, p < 0.001). Further fsQCA configuration analysis identified four configurations of high continuance intention (with a solution consistency rate of 0.811 and a coverage rate of 0.469), which can be grouped into three broader patterns based on their theoretical coherence: the “expectation confirmation-dominated” pattern (Configurations 1 and 2, with consistency rates of 0.855 and 0.839, respectively), the “full-dimensional attribute-driven” pattern (Configuration 3, consistency rate of 0.814), and the “Social-Hedonic Compensation” pattern (Configuration 4, consistency rate of 0.836), indicating substantial heterogeneity in continuance intention logic across different segments. Theoretically, this study extends the ECM-VAM framework to the context of children’s embodied intelligent products by introducing visual aesthetics and technical reliability as context-specific antecedents of perceived value, demonstrates that unstructured online review texts can serve as a valid source for the contextualized operationalization of theoretical constructs, and qualifies the linear assumptions of conventional net-effect models through a configurational perspective.

candidates.title: Continuance Intention Towards AI-Enabled Fintech Services in India: Examining the Roles of Trust and Perceived Privacy Risk Method
candidates.abstract: With India’s rapid digital transformation driven by the Unified Payments Interface ecosystem and widespread adoption of AI-powered fintech services, such as Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm, understanding the determinants of users’ continuance intention has become increasingly critical. Despite extensive research on fintech adoption, post-adoption behavior and continuance usage of AI-enabled fintech services in emerging economies like India remain underexplored. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a comprehensive model integrating parasocial relationship theory, trust-commitment theory, UTAUT2, and the Service Robot Acceptance Model (sRAM). Survey data from 624 fintech AI users across Karnataka, India, provide rich insights into AI-enabled fintech service continuance in a rapidly digitizing economy. The findings reveal that performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, and social influence positively impact engagement and continuance intentions, with perceived intelligence and perceived accuracy also playing significant roles. The study establishes the moderating effect of perceived privacy risk on several key relationships, advancing the understanding of AI-enabled fintech service continuance in the Indian context.

candidates.title: Human–Robot Interaction in Industrial Contexts
candidates.abstract: Technological advances in industrial robotics have significantly changed modern working environments, enabling greater autonomy, flexibility and productivity. Here the emergence of advanced robots designed for direct interaction with humans play a substantial role. By integrating emerging technologies such as AI, machine learning, and sophisticated interaction design, advanced robots are reshaping industries. All while increasing efficiency and customization and remaining cost-effective. Despite their benefits, the use of robotic systems also brings challenges, particularly in the area of occupational safety and health. After an overview of the evolution of different robotic systems, a description of industrial work tasks, related working conditions and highlighted risk and opportunities associated with automation, this chapter examines key safety factors that are essential for close human–robot interaction and assesses their impact on workers. Two case studies illustrate how the practical application of advanced robotic systems in industrial settings affects workplace dynamics. The chapter further highlights the role of worker expectations and experience in relation to advanced robotics. By combining empirical evidence with real-world applications, this chapter underscores the importance of adaptable, user-friendly robotic systems that prioritize worker well-being alongside operational efficiency. In doing so, it contributes to the broader dialogue on sustainable, ergonomic innovation in the workplace and highlights the critical role of human-centered design in the future of industrial robotics.

candidates.title: Challenges and design requirements for public-facing social robots
candidates.abstract: Public-facing social robots are increasingly being introduced into environments such as airports, libraries, hospitals, and campuses to provide information, assistance, and engagement. Their operation in these open and dynamic settings introduces complex challenges that cut across privacy, cybersecurity, ethics, usability, and regulation. While existing studies have explored these dimensions separately, few have examined how they intersect in real-world deployments. This study draws on semi-structured interviews with twenty-one multidisciplinary experts to identify cross-cutting risks and practical design requirements for public-facing social robots. Thematic analysis identified interrelated challenges concerning technical capabilities, public interaction, and organisational conditions, including risks associated with third-party components. Experts emphasized privacy- and security-by-design principles, adaptive and inclusive interaction, resilient technical architectures, and certification mechanisms for responsible deployment. The study’s contribution is a context-specific synthesis that organizes these established engineering and governance principles around the conditions of public-facing deployment. The resulting requirements and indicators are presented as candidate guidance for subsequent operationalization and validation, rather than as validated engineering standards.

candidates.title: Mutual Adaptation and Influence: Review of Latent Dynamics Models in Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in robotics have enabled more dynamic and interactive roles when working with humans. This progress is enabled in part by latent state models, which allow the robot to predict human actions in a compact and tractable way. This paradigm has allowed robots not only to respond and adapt to human behavior but also to anticipate and plan proactively through the use of latent dynamics models. This review explores the use of such models in the field of human–robot interaction. Existing literature reveals three classes of latent dynamics models: Bayesian, Markovian, and encoded. To connect these works, we synthesize a unified framework consisting of a prediction and control step. This framework shows how the traditional one‐way adaptation extends to mutually adaptive behaviors by using latent dynamics in the prediction step. Similarly, we show how influence is an extension of mutual adaptation by using latent dynamics in the control step. We then review state‐of‐the‐art approaches to mutual adaptation and influence for the three latent dynamics classes and discuss emergent properties as they relate to application, update frequency, and specific considerations for mutual adaptation or influence. Using this review, we highlight gaps in the current literature and propose future directions.

candidates.title: Advances in Robot Visual Gesture Interaction Technology from a Bio-Inspired and Machine Learning Perspective
candidates.abstract: As robots increasingly enter open environments such as collaborative manufacturing, public services, and assisted care, the ability to accurately perceive human behavioral cues and interaction intentions has become a crucial foundation for advanced human-computer interaction systems. Visual gestures possess distinct characteristics, including non-contact operation, clear spatial orientation, and low interaction burden. However, their practical applications remain significantly affected by complex backgrounds, partial occlusions, individual user differences, and real-time computing constraints. This comprehensive article reviews robot visual gesture interaction technology from the innovative perspective of integrating biological visual attention mechanisms with modern machine learning paradigms. First, the biologically inspired mechanisms and their computational representations, such as selective attention, saliency drive, and attention focus, are systematically outlined. Subsequently, the main technological routes—including artificial features with traditional machine learning, deep feature learning, keypoint sequential modeling, and advanced attention-based structural models—are thoroughly summarized, and their specific applicable conditions and inherent limitations are critically compared. Furthermore, the specific application requirements and evaluation dimensions across diverse scenarios, such as industrial collaboration, service and social robots, and assistive robotics, are deeply analyzed. Existing research clearly demonstrates that this dynamic field is rapidly expanding from simple single-frame action classification to complex spatio-temporal feature fusion and contextual intent understanding. Ultimately, achieving open environment robustness, cross-user generalization, real-time lightweight processing, multi-modal fusion, and stringent safety and reliability remains the primary focus of subsequent research endeavors in this domain.

candidates.title: “Cute Companion” or “Awful Thing”: Understanding individual differences in attitudes to social robots as pets
Digital Human Modeling in Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: In human–robot collaboration, there are different levels of interaction. At lower levels, collisions must be avoided. At a higher level, collaborative robots directly interact with humans, and human health and safety need to be assured when designing work systems with robots included. In the process, adequate models of human motions are required. The diversity of human motions has led to ongoing research activities that have provided a considerable range of models. This chapter provides an overview of full-body human models such as kinematics, dynamics, and skin models and their applications in robotics. Kinematic models provide an abstraction of the human skeleton structure and its joints, whereas skin models provide mappings from the skeleton models to skin surfaces. Both are required for motion simulation with most human motion models. A survey of analytical, physics and data-driven human motion models is given. The state of the art as well as recent research advances are summarized for the models, and models of singular human motions and motion corridor/density models are differentiated. Their relevance for different levels of human–robot collaboration and ergonomics is discussed. Applications of motion models in the collaborative robotics domain and their respective advantages and shortcomings are reviewed with a special focus on their applicability for safety, efficiency and user experience in digital twins. Finally, the chapter presents three application scenarios in assembly lines and material handling in automotive industry.

candidates.title: Quantifying the Subjective Experience in Human–Robot Interaction
candidates.abstract: Assessing the quality of interaction between collaborative robots (i.e., cobots) and humans to achieve a (shared) goal is an essential part of supporting the diffusion of usable and safe collaborative robotic systems. The key issue here is that cobots within and between domains can vary substantially in terms of features even when these are meant to support similar tasks. Under this perspective, it seems very hard, if not impossible, to identify coherent ways to benchmark the quality of cobots. However, all the cobots share one element which is that they have to deal with humans and satisfy them. This chapter claims that focusing on how a system can satisfy the human counterpart can (indirectly) provide insights into the quality of cobots that can be a piece of valuable information for the designers. In this sense, identifying and validating a set of key aspects to assess the subjective experience in interaction with robots during collaborative tasks is a stepping stone for benchmarking cobots. We will discuss how, in other domains, researchers developed standardized scales to ensure comparable results regarding the user experience (UX), and to model the differences between systems. Moreover, based on a recent systematic literature review, an initial list of key aspects to evaluate UX with cobots is discussed as a step to build and validate a future tool for unifying how experts evaluate cobots.

candidates.title: Mapping older adults´ use of social robots: An institutional ethnographic perspective
candidates.abstract: Technology has been seen as a solution to the challenges related to the care of older adults, and it is possible to talk about “the ageing-and-innovation discourse” (Neven & Peine, 2017). This study used institutional ethnography to explore the presence of the discourse in a care home in Finland. A map of the discourse was produced from the viewpoint of older adults who participated in robot workshops, by interacting with the robots and discussing about them, in the care home. The analysis of Finnish policy documents revealed an overarching discourse on aging and innovation, in which technology was linked to economic growth, public sector efficiency, and improved access to care. The participants placed themselves on the map as learners, users and innovators of technology. The researchers were viewed as sources of information, care workers as enablers of robot use and engineers as designers of robots. The robots were viewed as having instrumental value and as objects to be utilised.

candidates.title: Potential and limitations of socially assistive robots to support malnutrition care: a critical reflection by dietitians
candidates.abstract: Nutrition is essential for the physical and psychological well-being and health of older adults. Malnutrition negatively affects both their physical and mental health and their overall quality of life. Dietitians face challenges in supporting older adults due to time constraints, which can limit the continuity of care. While previous research highlights the potential of assistive technologies to help reduce malnutrition, such as socially assistive robots (SARs), these approaches lack a holistic perspective and insufficiently address collaborative processes within the broader care network. This study presents the findings from a Research-through-Design (RtD) study in which eight dietitians from four practices participated in context-mapping sessions involving personas, generative design probes, ranking exercises, and speculative design activities to critically reflect on the potential role of socially assistive robots in supporting collaborative malnutrition care. The results were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. These results highlight key challenges in nutritional care, including the social nature of eating, the need for personalized support, and challenges within the care network. These findings informed potential roles for SARs, including reinforcing dietary advice, supporting shared decision-making, facilitating collaboration, and encouraging shared eating moments. Crucially, the findings suggest that the value of SARs depends less on adding new functionalities than on carefully positioning their role within collaborative nutritional care. This includes preserving older adults' autonomy, clearly allocating responsibilities between dietitians and technology, supporting meaningful engagement between consultations, and maintaining appropriate professional boundaries.

candidates.title: Data for: Same Character, Forgotten Owner? Behavioral Continuity and Data-Deletion Judgments in Companion Robot Handover
candidates.abstract: This dataset accompanies the manuscript “Same Character, Forgotten Owner? Behavioral Continuity and Data-Deletion Judgments in Companion Robot Handover.” It contains de-identified participant-level and trial-level data from a formative interview study (n = 24), a 2 × 2 experiment (500 completers), and an interface experiment (512 completers; 4,096 case judgments). The workbook includes enrollment and attrition records, translated interview excerpts and coding fields, pilot records, Study 2 responses, Study 3 participant and case-level records, participant summaries, and reported statistical results. The studies examine how continuity of a companion robot’s expressive behavior affects judgments about residual personal data, and whether a separated handover interface improves probability judgments while preserving perceived identity continuity.

candidates.title: How metaverse influencers shape electronic word-of-mouth: Credibility, attractiveness, and parasocial relationships across cultures and gender
candidates.abstract: Metaverse Influencers (MVIs) are technologically constructed social actors increasingly promoting tourism destinations. However, they continue to be viewed as uncannily or authentically fake, raising questions about whether followers perceive them as credible, form meaningful parasocial relationships with them, and intend to recommend the destinations they endorse. To address these gaps, this study integrated source credibility theory, parasocial relationship theory, and the similarity-attractiveness model and tested a framework linking source credibility and physical attractiveness to e-WOM intentions, with parasocial relationship as the mediator. Using a quantitative design across three cases (main effects/mediation; UK–USA–India; female–male), results showed that parasocial relationships increased e-WOM, and source credibility increased both parasocial relationships and e-WOM. Physical attractiveness did not directly increase e-WOM, but strengthened parasocial relationships, which fully mediated the attractiveness–e-WOM link; mediation was partial for credibility. Only one cross-country difference emerged (attractiveness to e-WOM was stronger in the USA), and one gender difference (attractiveness to parasocial relationship stronger for males). These findings show that the extent to which MVIs influence their followers is not only dependent upon the designed appearance of the MVI itself but also on whether followers perceive them as credible and develop parasocial relationships with them. The study enhances our knowledge of human relationships with synthetic social actors and provides insights into how MVIs should be created to responsibly promote tourism communications.

candidates.title: Integrating Social Robotics into School AAC Practices: A Hybrid Architecture for Pedagogically Mediated Communicative Participation
candidates.abstract: Functional use of Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) by students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) remains a central challenge in Multifunctional Resource Rooms. This article presents a hybrid system integrating the NAO robot as a pedagogical mediator into existing school AAC practices. Built under the Design Science Research framework, the system addresses the technical heterogeneity among the AAC resources already in use by students. Applied across ten sessions with three children with ASD, with teachers co-planning all interactions, results showed progression in autonomous AAC use, including generalization to natural contexts such as the school's Science Fair. This suggests integrating social robotics with existing practices is a productive path toward inclusive participation.

candidates.title: CreaRobot - Improving creativity using a social robot
candidates.abstract: Supporting children’s creativity in educational settings remains a key challenge, which generative AI-powered social robots may help address. This paper presents CreaRobot, a study in which children performed a standardized drawing task while interacting with a social robot driven by a vision-language model. We compared two conditions: a generic feedback condition, in which the robot produced pre-recorded generic compliments, and a contextualized feedback condition, in which the robot engaged in structured interaction phases grounded in a real-time visual analysis of each child’s drawing. Results from 49 participants show that contextualized feedback significantly improved the value of the creative product (M = 21.52 vs. M = 13.85; Cohen’s d = 1.34), with a large effect size. These preliminary findings suggest that grounding a social robot’s feedback in real-time perception of the creative process is a promising direction for AI-supported creativity in educational settings.

candidates.title: Understanding Older Adults’ And Caretakers’ Attitudes Toward Social Robots Using Natural Language Processing and Thematic Analysis
candidates.abstract: Abstract The present study aims to examine the role of social robots in enriching older adults’ environments and helping them cope with the problems that decrease their well-being and life quality. To understand how social robots can be integrated into older adults’ lives, we investigated both older adults’ and caretakers’ attitudes toward social robots. For this aim, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 participants. In these interviews, we showed them photos and videos of the three social robots with different looks, abilities, and degrees of resemblance to humans. Then, we asked them to answer some open-ended questions. These robots were the pet-like robot Aibo, the toy-like robot Paro, and the humanoid robot Pepper. We analyzed the answers using complementary quantitative and qualitative approaches. The quantitative approach included the Sentiment Analysis (SA) and the qualitative approach included the Thematic Analysis (TA). SA results indicate that caretakers approached negatively to Paro, and positively to Aibo and Pepper. On the other hand, older adults did not differ in the polarity of attitudes toward the three robots. The TA results yielded four overarching themes: I) Perceived and expected roles of the robot, II) Physical characteristics and design features of the robot, III) Factors influencing acceptance of the robot, and IV) Disadvantages of the robot. Under those, there were various themes and sub-themes diversified for each robot. Overall, our findings reveal significant insights into older adults’ and caretakers’ approaches to different types of social robots and enable researchers to use these robots more effectively.

candidates.title: OpenWater Hub: An open-source hardware platform for marine robotics support and water quality data acquisition
candidates.abstract: At present, there is no single open-source electronic hardware platform that natively integrates 24 V industrial RS485 sensors with marine robotic and hydroponic actuation. Consequently, hardware fragmentation exists severely in underwater sensing and environmental monitoring. Researchers using benchtop calibration must purchase closed-source ecosystems with proprietary operating systems, limiting the use of custom control loops. Conversely, open-source embedded systems provide optimized low-voltage passive monitoring but lack sufficient power for heavy actuators. The OpenWater Hub (OWH) provides a centralized platform for these two areas to exist on one printed circuit board (PCB). The PCB features a 24 V pass-through bus that supports the heavy inrush currents of industrial RS-485 probes. A dual-ATmega128A topology is utilized to prevent serial polling delays from disrupting real-time motor control. The architecture consists of one chip that isolates Modbus communication for sub-millisecond parsing, and another chip that drives soft robotic fish and actuators via four 3.0 A PWM channels. The core board is configured to transform across four deployment variants: a benchtop logger, a portable field laboratory, an autonomous floating station, and a tethered robotic support hub. Modular UART sockets support telemetry via LoRa, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular modules. The static baseline power consumption was 196.4 mW; after 240 h of thermal testing, the OpenWater Hub demonstrated > 99.97 % telemetry reliability and logged chemical validations yielding a 0.9903 correlation coefficient value. Documentation and C++ logic files for the reproduction of all deployment variants are included.

candidates.title: TEIDAN: A Multilingual Multiparty Dialogue Corpus
candidates.abstract: Multi-party interaction is a central setting for human communication and a necessary target for human-agent interaction systems that must participate in group conversation. Yet available corpora often focus on meetings, task-oriented interaction, text-based interaction, or acted scenarios, and fewer resources support cross-linguistic comparison of spontaneous face-to-face triadic discussion. This paper presents TEIDAN, a multilingual multimodal corpus that currently consists of Japanese and English three-party conversations. TEIDAN records groups of three participants discussing open-ended topics with individual pin microphones, a microphone array, and participant-facing cameras, and provides IPU-based transcripts for both language portions. Earlier studies used subsets of the Japanese portion for task-specific benchmarks in multi-party dialogue modeling; in contrast, this paper presents TEIDAN as a corpus resource spanning both Japanese and English, with planned expansion to additional languages. We describe the collection design, participants, recording setup, transcription format, and corpus statistics, and provide preliminary analyses to illustrate how TEIDAN can support research on turn-taking, addressee recognition, and multimodal grounding in human-human and human-agent interaction.

candidates.title: Dataset for Human–Robot Team Trust and Social Comparison Study
candidates.abstract: This dataset supports the study entitled "The Effects of Teammate Type on Trust in Human–Robot Teams from the Perspective of Social Comparison: The Roles of Interpersonal Expectations and Perceived Emotions". The dataset contains anonymized experimental data collected from 137 participants in a human–robot interaction study. The study investigated how teammate type and social comparison direction influence trust formation in human–robot teams. The dataset includes participant demographic information, experimental conditions, and measurements of cognitive trust, affective trust, interpersonal expectations, perceived emotions, and related trust variables. All data have been anonymized to protect participant privacy. The study was conducted in accordance with ethical principles and approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing University of Chemical Technology. The dataset is shared to support research transparency, verification, and future studies in human–robot interaction.

candidates.title: Videogame spectatorship and orbital fandom value
candidates.abstract: This thesis examines the layered and evolving nature of online videogame fandoms, with a particular focus on what it terms orbital fandom; fan communities that emerged one or more step removed from the original game text. Rather than engaging directly with the game itself, these fans form attachment through derivative content, content creators, and platform-medicated interactions. By shifting attention to these decentralised forms of engagement, the thesis expands existing models of fandom to account for the complex social, affective, and economic dynamics that shape participation in contemporary digital game cultures. To explore these dynamics, the research draws on a mixed-methods approach combining virtual ethnography, semi-structured stakeholder interviews, and a participant journaling study. This methodology allows for both creator- and viewer-centred perspectives, capturing how value; cultural, social, and monetary is produced, circulated, and contested within platformed fan ecosystems. The thesis develops the Orbital Fandom Framework, a conceptual model that articulates how these forms of fandom operate within the wider infrastructures of platform governance and digital labour. Empirical findings reveal how fan labour often takes place under informal, precarious, and frequently unacknowledged conditions. At the same time, fan contributions, particularly within orbital fandoms, play a vital role in shaping visibility, community cohesion, and even commercial success within the games industry. The thesis also explores the emotional intensities of parasocial relationships and the ethical concerns surrounding platform incentives and exploitation. These findings hold relevance not only for academic debates in game and fan studies but also for developers and platform designers seeking to engage with fan communities in more ethical and inclusive ways. By introducing a new conceptual vocabulary, advancing a critical framework, and offering practical insights, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the socio-cultural and economic life of videogame fandoms in the platform era.

candidates.title: Hardware implementation of AI-based fuzzy logic for real-time sign language interpreter robotic control using FPGA
candidates.abstract: Abstract Communication barriers between hearing-impaired individuals and non-sign language users remain a significant challenge in modern society. Existing sign language recognition systems primarily focus on unidirectional communication and are often limited by high latency, excessive power consumption, and lack of robustness in uncertain environments. This paper proposes a novel FPGA-based Bidirectional Robotic Sign Language Communication System (BRSLCS) integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI), fuzzy logic, and robotic control for real-time assistive communication. The proposed architecture supports both forward communication, where sign language gestures are translated into text or speech, and reverse communication, where text or speech is converted into robotic sign language gestures through an actuated robotic hand. In the forward communication flow, gesture images captured using a camera are processed through preprocessing, feature extraction, AI-based classification, and fuzzy inference stages. In the reverse communication flow, speech or textual inputs are interpreted using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and mapped into robotic sign gestures controlled using FPGA-based actuation logic. The integration of fuzzy logic improves classification robustness and interpretability under uncertain conditions such as illumination variation, gesture ambiguity, and motion blur. FPGA implementation provides deterministic timing, low latency, hardware parallelism, and energy efficiency suitable for embedded real-time systems. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed system achieves 92-95% recognition accuracy with latency between 10-25 ms while consuming only 4-6 W power, outperforming conventional CPU and GPU-based implementations. The proposed BRSLCS provides a scalable and practical framework for inclusive communication systems in healthcare, education, public services, and human-robot interaction environments.

candidates.title: Interactions
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores the diverse interaction modalities that are involved in human–robot interaction (HRI) through extended reality (XR). These interactions enable communication and collaboration between humans and robots. It deals with physical and haptic interaction, as well as gesture- and movement-based interaction. Apart from this, it also deals with voice, gaze, and controller-based interfaces. The environmental, spatial, and tangible interactions are also discussed in the context of embodied and situated action. The chapter also addresses multimodal and adaptive interaction strategies that combine multiple input and feedback channels. It also deals with collaborative, social, autonomous, and instruction-based interaction paradigms. This chapter, therefore, deals with selecting and designing interaction modalities that are effective, intuitive, and context-aware within XR-enabled HRI systems.

candidates.title: IntentVLM: Open-Vocabulary Intention Recognition through Forward–Inverse Modeling with Video-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Improving the effectiveness of human–robot interaction requires social robots to accurately infer human goals through robust intention understanding. This challenge is particularly critical in multimodal settings, where agents must integrate heterogeneous signals including text, visual cues to form a coherent interpretation of user intent. This paper presents IntentVLM, a novel two-stage video-language framework designed for open-vocabulary human intention recognition. The approach is inspired by forward-inverse modeling in cognitive science by decomposing intention understanding into goal candidate generation followed by structured inference through selection, effectively reducing hallucinations in latent reasoning. Evaluated on the IntentQA and Inst-IT Bench datasets, IntentVLM achieves state-of-the-art results with up to 80% accuracy, notably surpassing the baseline performance by 30% and matches human performance. Our findings demonstrate that this structured reasoning approach enhances open-vocabulary intention understanding without catastrophic forgetting, offering a robust foundation for human-centered robotics.

candidates.title: Social Structural Pressures and East Asian Adolescents' Consumption Behaviors Toward Virtual Anime-Style Characters: The Mediating Role of Parasocial Attachment
candidates.abstract: East Asian adolescents face multiple structural stressors, including academic pressure, peer competition, parental expectations, and uncertainty about the future. When these pressures frustrate their basic psychological needs, some turn to virtual anime-style games for emotional compensation, forming parasocial attachments to virtual characters. Integrating compensatory consumption theory and parasocial relationship theory, this paper synthesizes existing literature to construct an analytical pathway from structural social stress through psychological need deficits and parasocial attachment to consumption behavior. The analysis suggests that when academic competition and family expectations leave adolescents' needs for belongingness and competence unfulfilled, their emotional involvement with virtual characters accelerates from casual contact toward attachment; once attachment is formed, consumption becomes a natural extension of maintaining and expressing the relationship, manifested both in the general logic of paying for parasocial proximity and in possessiveness-driven consumption that transforms intangible bonds into tangible possessions. Moreover, the developmental asynchrony between the socioemotional system and the cognitive control system during adolescence further heightens adolescents' susceptibility to immediate rewards in gaming contexts. By integrating compensatory consumption theory and parasocial relationship theory within the novel context of anime-style virtual games, this study extends the application boundaries of both frameworks, and suggests that parents and schools should attend to the real-world satisfaction of adolescents' needs for autonomy, competence, and belonging rather than merely restricting gaming time and spending.

candidates.title: CEMIR vs. FISER: a comparative study of reasoning-based and enrichment-based approaches to pragmatic intent recognition
candidates.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.

candidates.title: Real-World Emotion Recognition Using Edge AI
candidates.abstract: The education sphere, healthcare, automotive safety, social robots, and smart technology sectors require emotion recognition through speech and facial expressions. Nonetheless, deep learning technologies are based on cloud computing which results in longer response times and needs data storage that fits sensitive data for transfer. With Edge AI, it becomes possible to perform inference in the proximity of the sensing device. This paper aims to explore lightweight architecture types and implementation techniques implementing emotion recognition at the edge. The types of architecture and techniques discussed throughout the paper include small CNNs, transformer-based models, and deep learning model compression methods, as quantization, pruning, knowledge engineering, and NAS. The article discusses a comparison between the types of implementations used for the technologies (embedded hardware and inference frameworks) and forms of optimization techniques. In addition, it compares the various studies that have been conducted on them regarding their implementation, type of data sets, and effectiveness, including the ones that failed to mention the latency of their system.

candidates.title: Conditions and Pathways for Integrating Smart Care Robots Into Long-Term Care Facilities: Qualitative Study From Nursing Assistants’ Perspectives
candidates.abstract: Background: Smart care robots are increasingly viewed as a potential way to address care burden and support care quality in long-term care facilities. However, their integration into routine care practice remains limited, and the conditions required for their effective implementation are not yet well understood from the perspective of frontline nursing assistants. Objective: This study aimed to clarify nursing assistants' core functional expectations of smart care robots in long-term care facilities and to explore the key conditions for their integration into practice. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted. Using purposive sampling, 31 frontline nursing assistants were recruited from 5 long-term care facilities in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China, with recruitment assistance from facility administrators and eligibility screening by the research team. Semistructured face-to-face interviews were conducted between September and November 2025. Data were analyzed using framework analysis. Results: Framework analysis produced 4 analytical domains: real-world care needs, limited facilitating conditions, major anticipated barriers, and preparatory pathways for implementation. Participants expected robots to support safety monitoring and risk warning, standardized checking and management, repetitive physical tasks, and basic interaction. Although some openness to technology and organizational support existed, these facilitating conditions were insufficient for routine implementation. Key barriers included unclear human-robot collaboration models, inadequate organizational capacity, potential new care risks, and weak external support. Participants emphasized organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, pilot testing, and structured training as essential preparatory steps. Emotional support functions were also valued for alleviating caregivers' emotional burden in high-intensity care work. Conclusions: Openness to technology, supportive organizational climates, and positive policy and social signals provided an initial foundation for considering robot integration. However, uncertainties remained around human-robot collaboration, risk management, organizational capacity, and concrete external support. Organizational assessment, contextual adaptation, real-world pilot testing, and practical training warrant further evaluation before wider implementation.

candidates.title: Security and Privacy‐Preserving Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: This work examines the privacy and security issues with tiny machine learning (TinyML) and proposes potential solutions to improve dependability and trust in practical applications. A thorough analysis of current security risks is conducted, including data leakage, model extraction, and adversarial assaults. Furthermore, their suitability for TinyML environments is examined for privacy-preserving strategies, including secure enclaves, federated learning, and differential privacy. Because of their limited resources, TinyML systems present particular security and privacy issues that reduce the efficacy of conventional defences. New approaches to reducing these concerns, like decentralized learning, safe model deployment, and lightweight encryption, appear promising. This study offers a thorough examination of privacy and security concerns unique to TinyML, a comparatively unexplored subject within the larger field of artificial intelligence (AI) security. It advances secure edge AI research by bridging the gap between TinyML restrictions and contemporary security solutions.

candidates.title: Hands, Keys, or Joysticks: Comparing Control Interfaces for Tangible Social Interactions in Remote Presence Robots
candidates.abstract: Abstract Advances in telerobotic platforms promise to transform human-robot interaction, yet identifying effective control interfaces for operating robotic manipulators onboard telerobots with the goal of increasing tangible interaction capabilities remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the development and comparative analysis of three control interfaces for operating manipulators onboard a social mobile remote presence platform, Quori. The control interfaces include computer vision (CV) guided gesture control, traditional keyboard input, and joystick manipulation via a gaming controller. These control methods were designed to support pilot users in executing primary social interaction tasks including greetings (e.g. handwave), contact interactions (e.g. fist bump and high five), and referencing (e.g. alert and point). To investigate the efficacy of these interfaces, we conducted a within-subjects study ( N = 30) comparing the different control interfaces in a mock social scenario between a pilot user and a confederate local user. Quantitative performance of pilot users was assessed by measuring task completion time and error counts, while qualitative evaluations of user satisfaction, perceived control intuitiveness, and workload were obtained via standardized instruments (NASA Task Load Index (TLX), System Usability Scale (SUS), User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ)) and structured interviews. Results indicate that while keyboard input, closely followed by CV gesture control, delivered the fastest completion times and highest perceived task effectiveness; CV gesture control maximized engagement and overall user experience. These findings offer valuable insights into optimizing human-robot interaction and inform future designs of telerobotic control systems across various application domains.

candidates.title: Message Over Modality: Toward a Source-Agnostic Message Evaluation Framework for AI-Delivered Social Support
candidates.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly take on socially supportive roles, questions remain about how users perceive such support across different AI modalities (i.e., the form through which an AI system communicates, such as voice, embodiment, or text). This study examines early-stage evaluations formed after a single initial interaction with three common AI modalities, voice-based assistants (VBAs), social robots, and text-based generative AI, delivering either informational or emotional support. Using a 3 (AI modality: VBA vs. social robot vs. text-based generative AI) × 2 (support type: emotional vs informational) between-subjects experimental design, participants (N = 203) viewed scripted video vignettes of human–AI encounters and then evaluated the AI agents on credibility (competence, character, caring), task and social attraction, and perceived support. Results revealed that all agents were rated significantly above the midpoint on most attributes, suggesting users accept AI agents as credible and supportive. However, no significant differences emerged between AI types. Instead, support type had a stronger influence; informational support increased perceived competence, while emotional support elevated perceptions of caring. Qualitative responses supported these trends, emphasizing message relevance over agent form. These findings introduce and support the Source-Agnostic Message Evaluation (SAME) framework, which proposes that in early-stage, observational AI support contexts, users assess AI support based more on what is said than who, or what, says it. This has implications for AI design, emphasizing message quality over modality in user experience optimization.

candidates.title: ARAM: a threshold model for understanding occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations
candidates.abstract: Physical interior elements are increasingly becoming roboticised to support occupant needs. Partitions, ceilings, and furniture can now physically and autonomously change shape or move to architecturally “adapt” indoor spaces, with the aim of improving occupant comfort, satisfaction, and wellbeing. However, occupants sometimes reject these adaptations when they are perceived as disruptive, unpredictable, or difficult to control. Motivated by the goal of making architectural robots more acceptable, we involved an interdisciplinary team of experts in human-building interaction, human-robot interaction, psychology, anthropology, and human comfort to qualitatively re-analyze how occupants accepted adaptations across three previous studies on robotic partitions. We found that an occupant tended to accept an adaptation when they recognized a personal need that the architectural robot was capable of addressing in a socially justifiable way. Accordingly, we developed the Architectural Robot Acceptance Model (ARAM), in which three qualitative thresholds along a continuum of perceived stress severity define four distinct acceptance responses to a specific adaptation. As the positions of these thresholds may vary across occupants and situations, ARAM supports testable estimates of how an occupant may respond to different appraisal states of personal need, adaptation capability, and social justification. Because architectural robot adaptations may simultaneously be experienced as robotic behaviors, building automation, and socially situated environmental adjustments, ARAM is particularly relevant to individual adaptations that enter occupants' spatial experience and may affect co-located others. We then discuss how the model can inform situated estimates of occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations, and outline how its broader relevance to other robotic, automated, intelligent, and smart technologies embedded in the built environment may be evaluated in future work.

candidates.title: RoboMMT: Learning Stable Tracking of Modulated Expressive and Interactive Robot Motion
candidates.abstract: Expressive robot motion can improve naturalness, effectiveness, and perceived likability in human-robot interaction. When deployed on dynamically unstable platforms, however, reactive execution of expressive body motion may bring the robot to its stability limits, especially when expressivity is decoupled from physical control. In this paper, we present RoboMMT (Robot Modulated Motion Tracking), a modular control architecture that couples parameterized expressive motion synthesis, physics-based character control, and reactive adaptation to spatial interaction goals. Our approach trains a reference-conditioned tracking policy across a broad domain of expressivity, enabling it to faithfully realize the commanded motions while maintaining dynamic stability. Goal reactivity is achieved by training lightweight, task-specific interaction policies that modulate the reference generator's spatial goal-attraction point, with the stabilizing tracking policy kept in the loop. Evaluations on a quadruped and two humanoid robots show that the learned tracker remains stable and accurate across the entire modulation domain, whereas trackers trained without this coverage lose balance, tracking accuracy, or both. We show that layering closed-loop goal adaptation over this foundation enables interactive facing and pointing behaviors, while maintaining stable execution and comparable reference-tracking fidelity. The robot learns to proactively redistribute its weight and take corrective steps. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated through real-robot experiments on a quadruped under heavy disturbances.

candidates.title: Ergonomics, Robotics, and Disciplinary Integration
candidates.abstract: Ergonomics is inherently based on disciplinary integration: a compulsory condition to lead the systemic understanding and improvement of real-world complexities like the ones of Human-Robot Interactions (HRIs). Accordingly, this chapter ponders the contributions of diverse disciplines to the study of human factors alongside their synergies with the multi-faceted area of robotics. Key examples are presented, considering problems requiring approaches like bio-inspired soft robotics, value-sensitive design, interactions and affective features, and neuroergonomics in HRI. The implications about education on HRI ergonomics are also pondered. Overall, this chapter remarks how diverse backgrounds can lead to contributions to the human-centered design and assessment of robots if the experts, regardless of disciplinary boundaries, just focus on learning novel perspectives and methods to solve the problems occurring in Human-Robot Systems.

candidates.title: Physical Ergonomics in Robotics
candidates.abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.

candidates.title: Mixed emotions evoked when incongruent outward appearance and motion are combined
candidates.abstract: Understanding mixed emotions is crucial for capturing the ambivalence of human information processing. However, how specific visual factors, such as outward appearance and motion, interact to evoke these conflicting feelings remains unclear. Here, we present three-dimensional (3D) characters as visual stimuli that evoke mixed feelings, providing empirical insights into emotional phenomena such as "kimo-kawaii" by focusing on their outward appearances and motions. Congruent stimuli (e.g., pleasant appearance with pleasant motion) and incongruent stimuli (e.g., pleasant appearance with unpleasant motion) were evaluated. Characters with congruent features evoked a single feeling: pleasant or unpleasant. In contrast, the combination of pleasant outward appearance and unpleasant motion evoked both pleasant and unpleasant feelings. Moreover, the combination of unpleasant outward appearance and pleasant motion strongly evoked unpleasant feelings rather than pleasant feelings. These findings suggest that, within the present stimulus set, outward appearance may exert a stronger influence on affective evaluation than motion. The observed co-activation of positive and negative affect may be relevant to mixed affective experiences such as "kimo-kawaii," although further research using construct-specific measures is needed to establish this relationship.
