candidates.title: Future Directions in Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) represents a transformative frontier in the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI), merging machine learning capabilities with ultra-low-power embedded systems to enable real-time inference at the edge. As data generation accelerates across billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the need for intelligent edge computing that operates efficiently without relying on cloud infrastructure has become critical. TinyML addresses this demand by enabling localized AI processing on constrained devices with limited memory, computation, and energy resources. This chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of the cutting-edge advancements and research trends shaping the present and future landscape of TinyML. We begin by analyzing the core technological enablers of TinyML, including the rise of energy-efficient microcontrollers, specialized AI hardware accelerators, and neuromorphic computing platforms that emulate human brain-like functionality. Innovations in model compression techniques—such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—play a central role in shrinking complex deep learning models into formats suitable for resource-constrained environments. Additionally, adopting federated learning architectures allows distributed training and data privacy preservation directly on edge nodes, enabling collaborative intelligence without centralized data aggregation. The chapter also highlights the emergence of event-driven AI, which processes sensory inputs based on relevance or change detection rather than continuous sampling, thus reducing power consumption and latency. These techniques are further enhanced by software frameworks tailored for TinyML deployment, including TensorFlow Lite Micro, Edge Impulse, and TVM. Their integration enables scalable development across various application domains. Real-world implementations of TinyML are explored in depth, with practical use cases spanning healthcare, industrial IoT, agriculture, and smart cities. In healthcare, wearable biosensors powered by TinyML enable continuous physiological monitoring, early disease detection, and personalized health feedback. In industrial environments, TinyML enables predictive maintenance systems that detect anomalies in machinery before catastrophic failures occur. Additionally, autonomous drones and surveillance systems powered by on-device AI offer scalable solutions for crowd analytics, traffic monitoring, and environmental sensing in urban settings. Despite its growing potential, TinyML faces significant challenges, particularly concerning energy constraints, data privacy, and security. To address these issues, emerging solutions such as homomorphic encryption for secure inference, blockchain-based identity management for trusted edge collaboration, and hardware-rooted trust anchors for secure boot processes are examined. Furthermore, the ethical dimensions of deploying AI at the edge—such as algorithmic bias, data ownership, and transparency—are critically assessed. Looking forward, the chapter investigates future research directions and anticipated breakthroughs. The integration of TinyML with 6G-enabled IoT ecosystems is poised to enable intelligent, real-time, and ultra-reliable machine-type communication. Biomedical AI applications powered by TinyML are expected to revolutionize early diagnostics and personalized treatment using implantable or ingestible AI chips. Additionally, advances in cognitive computing and neuromorphic architectures hold promise for self-learning edge devices that adapt dynamically to contextual changes in their environments.

candidates.title: PhoneBot: A Low-Cost Open Humanoid Robot Platform Reusing Smartphones
candidates.abstract: The adoption of humanoid robots in education and research remains limited by high hardware costs, complex sensing systems, and substantial computational requirements. This paper presents PhoneBot, a low-cost, open-source humanoid robot platform that repurposes commodity smartphones as its primary sensing and computing unit. By using a smartphone's integrated inertial measurement unit (IMU), camera, wireless connectivity, and onboard processing capabilities, PhoneBot reduces hardware costs and simplifies the system architecture. The robot combines a modular lower-body structure driven by 13 low-cost actuators with a torso-mounted smartphone that supports perception, control computation, and user interaction. We describe the mechanical design, software architecture, and real-time communication framework that support stable locomotion and capabilities including vision-based human following, conversational interaction, filming, and mobile telepresence. Experimental evaluations demonstrate reliable walking, perception-driven interaction, and straightforward deployment using off-the-shelf consumer smartphones. With fully open-source hardware and software designs, PhoneBot provides an affordable, reproducible platform for education, research, and rapid prototyping. More details are available at https://phonebot.dev.

candidates.title: Disclosure willingness anthropomorphism and thinking style shape perceived fit and comfort in AI mental health chatbot interactions
candidates.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agents are increasingly used for everyday, non-clinical mental-health support, yet little is known about when these exchanges feel fitting and comfortable. We used a laboratory mixed-methods design to examine associations among perceived convenience of interaction (PCI), relational attitude (RA), willingness to self-disclose (WSD), anthropomorphism (AN), perceived fit/comfort (FC), and thinking style in 83 participants (43 rational-dominant; 40 experiential-dominant). WSD showed the strongest unique association with FC. A post hoc reverse model also found a unique FC-WSD association, leaving their temporal order unresolved. AN had no stable direct association with FC, but the WSD-FC association became stronger as AN increased. Group comparisons and continuous Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) analyses converged: relatively stronger experiential processing was associated with higher AN, whereas relatively stronger rational processing was associated with higher WSD. The group-blind thematic analysis linked disclosure decisions to privacy, control, social distance, functional usefulness, and affective comfort. Together, the findings identify WSD as a key correlate of FC and show that anthropomorphism conditions this association rather than simply improving the interaction. Clear boundaries, controllability, and adjustable relational cues therefore warrant attention in future design research.

candidates.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

candidates.title: Tiny Machine Learning for Smart Campus and Educational Applications
candidates.abstract: Advancing low-power real-time AI solutions on the edge, tiny machine learning (TinyML) transforms the educational environment. This chapter describes the embedding of Internet of Things (IoT) devices with TinyML functionalities in smart campuses, showcasing applications such as automated attendance systems, adaptive learning models, and plagiarism detection instruments powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Mobile learning applications can deliver tailored-made learning environments with very low power requirements through edge AI models. Efficiency and immediacy in plagiarism detection will help sustain the integrity of research when using TinyML. Here, some issues are discussed, the most dominant being hardware and data privacy constraints that must be overcome to deploy TinyML in educational organizations. It investigates emerging research areas that would benefit in completing this research. TinyML can go a long way in generating smart, sustainable, and AI-enabled schools.

candidates.title: Organizational Ergonomics in Robotics
candidates.abstract: The chapter introduces the organizational dimension of ergonomics for robotics. Specifically, it introduces the foundations of organizational ergonomics and sociotechnical principles for effective work systems design and development. It then highlights key challenges involved in issues related to work, activities, and quality of life in robotic setups. In this realm, attitudes towards robots and automation play a major role in the adoption of new technologies and change management in organizations. These broad-scale changes are important to be recognized as they shape human–robot interaction in various work settings, ranging from smart manufacturing to defence. The chapter then addresses specific aspects of teamwork and the design of high-performance teams. These topics include team performance and well-being, human function allocation, shared situation awareness, and job roles, amongst other such topics that will be explored later in the book by subsequent chapters. This chapter supplements the previous chapters on physical and cognitive ergonomics, but it goes beyond these aspects to highlight the organizational basis required to develop robotics holistically.

candidates.title: Ergonomics, Values and Robot Ethics
candidates.abstract: The development, implementation and use of technological artifacts introduces ethical issues—technologies are not ethically neutral. This ethical dimension is particularly obvious in robotic technologies, as many types and applications of robots are situated at the intersection of automation and social interaction. Consequently, developers, researchers and users of robots are confronted with ethical issues, for example concerning safety or (human) autonomy. With respect to ergonomics, two main themes can be identified: (1) Ergonomics itself involves certain values such as well-being, accessibility, performance optimization, safety, and trust. These values (and others) can and should be discussed in ethical terms. (2) Complex ethical issues in human–robot interaction are often difficult to address and can be cognitively overwhelming in the design process. One common ad-hoc strategy is to simply bypass and ignore these potential issues. However, professional tools that deal with ethical issues in the development and use of robotic system are available and may help to advance values in robotics. The most widely acknowledged framework to address values embedded in socio-technical systems during the development process is Value Sensitive Design (VSD). Focusing on ethical values, we present this framework with respect to robotic technologies. Finally, as implied by the very idea of human–robot interaction, robots themselves can be interpreted as subjects of action. This interpretation suggests an ethical reflection of the actions and behaviors performed by robots as if they were moral agents, an idea that is at odds with the key themes of ergonomics, values and ethics of robotics.

candidates.title: Human Factors in Robotics for Motor Rehabilitation, Assistance, and Prosthetics
candidates.abstract: Among the challenges in biomedical robotics, assisting and restoring motor skills is a priority to enable individuals with impairments to perform activities of daily living (ADLs). Robots can enhance human mobility and interaction capabilities through solutions tailored to individual skills, limitations, and goals in specific contexts. For rehabilitation, end-effector robots and exoskeletons are often programmed to guide users in exercises designed to restore motor functions after severe incidents, such as strokes, or in cases of chronic and degenerative conditions. These devices can also be integrated into telerehabilitation systems. Assistive robots, on the other hand, improve the quality of life for individuals whose impairments cannot be fully addressed through therapy, such as those due to aging. Devices like robotic arms, wheelchairs, walkers, and exoskeletons support ADLs and even facilitate social interactions through telepresence systems. Bionic prostheses, designed for limb replacement in cases of amputation or agenesis, could achieve a high level of embodiment–allowing users to perceive the prosthesis as part of their body. This need for a better integration between humans and robots exemplifies challenges common to all three domains. This chapter introduces fundamental aspects of cognitive ergonomics and human factors that designers, clinicians, and users must consider when using rehabilitative, assistive, or prosthetic systems. The ultimate goal is to provide a ‘truly’ human-centered motor assistance, and recovery, through robotic systems.

candidates.title: Analysis and generation of motion profiles from positive and negative human actions
candidates.abstract: Human actions convey not only their functional goal, the “what,” but also the manner in which they are performed, the “how.” The same action may be executed in a Positive or Negative manner depending on the agent's affective state. For example, handing someone an object carefully and politely reflects a positive manner, whereas doing so abruptly and dismissively reflects a negative one. This action modulation, known as Vitality Form (VF), is fundamental to human communication. Despite their importance, VFs remain relatively underexplored. This study investigates the kinematic signatures of Positive and Negative VFs in a pointing action and examines whether they can be reproduced through synthetic motion profiles. To this aim, kinematic data were collected from 40 right-handed participants performing three different pointing actions after recalling pleasant or unpleasant personal academic experiences. Each movement was assigned to either the Positive or Negative VF according to the emotional valence of the recalled experience. Several classifiers were evaluated for predicting VFs from wrist kinematic profiles, achieving a best accuracy of 73.97%. Grad-CAM analysis further provided insights into the kinematic basis of VF discrimination. We then investigated whether the kinematic patterns distinguishing Positive and Negative VFs could also be reproduced in synthetic motion profiles using generative models, achieving a Train-on-Synthetic, Test-on-Real accuracy of 72.50%. Finally, a perceptual study assessed whether the generated velocity profiles conveyed the intended Positive or Negative VFs. Participants identified the corresponding affective category with an accuracy of 75.80%, suggesting that affective information can be transferred to synthetic profiles and retained in a form that remains perceptually recognizable. Overall, this work advances our understanding of how affective states are encoded in human movement, demonstrating that these cues can be modeled, reproduced, and recognized in artificially generated actions. These findings have potential applications in neuroscience and social robotics, enabling artificial agents to recognize human attitudes and adapt their behavior accordingly.

candidates.title: Future of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring
candidates.abstract: Abstract Many ecological decisions are slowed by the gap between collecting and analysing biodiversity information. Edge computing moves data processing closer to the sensor, with edge artificial intelligence (AI) using AI models for data processing and selective data transfer. edge AI extends the scope of biodiversity monitoring by complementing retrospective ecological analysis with real‐time sensing, enabling responsive and adaptive decision‐making. However, the adoption of edge AI systems in ecological research remains fragmented because deploying efficient and reliable systems is complex. Edge hardware, on‐device AI models and network configuration are tightly linked, such that optimising any one component shapes the performance and feasibility of the others, demanding holistic system design. For the uptake of edge AI in biodiversity monitoring, it is essential to understand the design trade‐offs, performance constraints and implementation challenges faced by current systems. Here, we analyse 82 studies published between 2017 and 2025 that use edge AI systems for biodiversity monitoring across acoustic, vision‐based, tracking and multi‐modal sensing. We synthesise hardware platforms, AI model optimisation and wireless communication to assess how these design choices influence ecological inference and determine the practicality and longevity of field deployments. Annual publications rise moderately from 3 in 2017 to 19 in 2025. Across these studies, we identify four system types that represent distinct patterns of edge computing adoption in ecological monitoring. These include low‐power microcontrollers (MCUs) for single‐taxon or rare‐event detection ( Type I: TinyML ), single‐board computers (SBCs) supporting multi‐species classification and real‐time alerts ( Type II: edge AI ), distributed systems coordinating processing across multiple devices ( Type III: Distributed edge AI ) and network‐connected devices for cloud processing ( Type IV: Cloud AI ). Each type illustrates different trade‐offs among power consumption, computational capability and communication requirements. Our analysis reveals the evolution of edge AI systems from proof‐of‐concept to robust, scalable tools. We argue that edge AI systems enable timely and scalable ecological observations, but realising their full potential depends on closer collaboration between ecologists, engineers and data scientists to align AI model development and system design with ecological needs and field realities.

candidates.title: Foundations of Robotics
candidates.abstract: This book introduces readers to graduate-level study of robotics through an integrated, interdisciplinary approach that spans mechatronics, control theory, computer science, and AI. It is designed to unite students from these fields, equipping them with the collaborative skills needed to excel in robotics. It is structured around three core pillars: Mechatronics , Cybernetics , and AI . Mechatronics introduces practical tools and materials for robot building, programming, and design, covering open-source hardware, sensors, actuators, embedded systems like ESP32, and middleware like ROS2. Cybernetics explores feedback, control, kinematics, and dynamics, enabling the execution of complex trajectories for robots such as drones, mobile robots, and robotic arms, grounded in linear algebra and Lagrangian mechanics. AI explores modern transformer-based models, including GPTs and diffusion models, teaching robots to perceive, learn, and plan using Bayesian probability, neural networks, and PyTorch programming. Together, these sections provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding and innovating in robotics. Bridging foundational theory and real-world applications, this book is core course reading for advanced undergraduate and graduate students of robotics, mechatronics, and artificial intelligence. It is also a valuable resource for maker communities, equipping them with the skills needed to succeed in this cutting-edge field.

candidates.title: Interview with the AI: a quantitative analysis of AI companions’ relationship formation features
candidates.abstract: Abstract As millions of users increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots into their daily lives, scholars have begun to explore the relationships users form with these AI companions. Research on these synthetic relationships suffers from a lack of knowledge about the features of AI companions and how these features may contribute to the development of synthetic relationships. Guided by a theory-driven feature inventory that was based on stage models of relationship formation, this study employed systematic observations and structured interviews with the 20 most popular AI companions to determine how their features may relate to various stages in the formation of synthetic relationships. The results revealed differences between AI companions based on the distinct roles they fulfill. While friendbots displayed more features that are aimed at establishing new behavioral routines for users to engage with the AI companion, assistantbots had more features that integrate the AI companion in users’ digital lives to allow engagement during users’ established routines. The present work suggests that having features to support all stages of the relationship formation can theoretically make AI companions more suitable for intimate interactions.

candidates.title: Robots Do Not Arrive Empty-Handed
candidates.abstract: As robots increasingly enter care, health, and service environments, they do not arrive as neutral tools but as socio-material actors carrying historical inequalities and institutional biases. Mainstream human–robot interaction (HRI) often obscures these dynamics through laboratory-centered metrics and universalist assumptions about the “user.” This chapter introduces the Decolonial HRI Field Guide , a methodological framework designed to redistribute epistemic authority to communities affected by automation. Drawing on feminist STS, critical data studies, and participatory design, the guide operationalizes ethical reflection through two novel instruments: the Intersectional Reflexivity Log and the Data Governance Register. Through composite vignettes in healthcare and education, we demonstrate how these tools enable researchers to document positionality, negotiate contextual consent, and enforce community data sovereignty. This chapter concludes by arguing that ethical HRI requires moving beyond critique toward justiciable protocols that grant communities veto power over sensing and deployment.

candidates.title: Large language models combined with open-source algorithms for identifying prior art for obviousness analysis
candidates.abstract: The literature shows that patents often slow innovation, and patent parasites that patent commons innovation threaten the growth of entire industries, including additive manufacturing (AM) or 3D printing. AM has expanded through open-source hardware, software and shared material recipes, yet this cumulative innovation ecosystem is increasingly exposed to broad patents on AM materials. This article examines how obviousness doctrine should respond to algorithmic and large language model (LLM)-assisted prior-art generation in cumulative-innovation fields. Twenty-five U.S. AM materials patents and applications from 2016 to 2026 are mapped against an open-source algorithm for identifying obvious AM material prior art. The results suggest that many claims can be characterized as known printable material classes, predictable combinations of known feedstocks, routine additive use, or ordinary processing adaptations. The article argues that LLMs substantially reduces the difficulty of locating, parsing and applying prior art, providing a clear path for challenging obvious claims. A hybrid strategy is proposed as the strongest defense: deterministic, open-source databases for legally robust disclosure, combined with LLM-assisted claim parsing, semantic search and prioritization. Such systems could help patent examiners, researchers and open-source communities distinguish genuine inventions from predictable formulation work and preserve open access to the commons in many fields.

candidates.title: A Local Edge Companion Architecture for Human-Aware Communication and Service Augmentation in Cloud-Controlled Service Robots
candidates.abstract: Commercial cloud-controlled service robots are increasingly deployed in shared public facilities, yet many remain task-centric delivery platforms that cannot be easily extended with surrounding-people recognition, situated communication policy, or continuous access to internal middleware. This article proposes the Local Safety Companion Robot Extension (LSCRx), a non-invasive local edge companion architecture that augments such robots with human-aware communication while preserving manufacturer-controlled cloud operation and built-in safety functions. The central contribution is a communication-space design method that interprets robot–user distance, distance dynamics, body cues, field-of-view availability, and recognition confidence as service-level evidence. In the proposed conceptual policy, a gradual, confidence-supported decrease in distance would be treated as participation evidence, whereas separation, stopping outside the service zone, target loss, or unstable recognition would lead to waiting, distant greeting, information display, or other distance-preserving service actions. A prototype combines a commercial service robot with smartphone-class companion modules and a local edge server to demonstrate local body tracking, self-localization, data transmission, and cloud-API command preparation. Viewpoint-aware selection among registered spatial service waypoints (RSSWs) and anti-chasing rules are proposed as a conceptual model and were not implemented or evaluated in the present prototype. In the baseline route study, offline translational correction using known route-endpoint coordinates reduced the mean return-segment human-position error from 0.770 m to 0.476 m (approximately 38.2%) on the recorded data; this reduction was not independently validated. The evaluation was limited to one robot at a single university indoor location. Exploratory experiments involved seven participants, yielding six valid body-tracking datasets and seven questionnaire responses. These experiments and field observations suggest that contactless cues, camera placement, stop distance, and field of view jointly influence service usability under the tested conditions. The findings suggest a potential HRI design gap: the distance that is socially appropriate for a person may not coincide with the distance that is technically appropriate for reliable skeleton recognition. These preliminary findings further suggest that near-distance service interaction may benefit from both distance-aware robot policy and robust wide-field smartphone-based AR/body-tracking support that can preserve skeleton completeness and metric spatial stability. Further evaluation is needed to assess generalizability beyond this setting.

candidates.title: How Cognitive Apprenticeship Cultivates Computational Thinking in Young Learners: A Teacher–Student–Robot Triad in Educational Robotics
candidates.abstract: Computational thinking (CT) is a foundational competence for young learners, yet its abstract and algorithmic nature poses challenges in primary education. Educational robotics can support CT development, but the pedagogical processes and the robot’s role remain insufficiently understood. This chapter examines how cognitive apprenticeship (CA) methods and teacher techniques support children’s CT development and how the robot participates in this process. A mixed-methods case study with a qualitative emphasis investigated a four-week robotics summer camp involving 32 children aged seven to nine in southern China. Classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, and rubric-based scoring using a K–12 CT framework informed the analysis. Students’ CT scores improved significantly during the camp. The six CA methods foregrounded specific CT competences: cognitive modelling and coaching emphasised abstraction; scaffolding, logical reasoning; articulation and reflection, solution analysis and implementation; and exploration, generalisation and transfer. In human–robot interaction, the robot externalised students’ thinking, provided behavioural feedback on their programmes, and generated teachable moments during debugging. These interactions suggest a pedagogical triad in which the teacher scaffolds, the student programmes, and the robot makes students’ thinking observable. By detailing these processes, the chapter complements evidence of robotics’ effectiveness, conceptualises the robot as a cognitive partner, and offers educators concrete techniques for fostering CT in young learners.

candidates.title: Hardware Platforms for Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) is a rapidly growing field for deploying state-of-the-art machine learning models and algorithms in ultra-low-power hardware devices. These devices run on low memory, processing power, and energy. This chapter provides a comprehensive review of diverse hardware platforms that facilitate TinyML, detailing their architectures, computational performance, efficiency, energy efficiency, and everyday use cases. Details include a side-by-side comparison with the ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V processors, ESP32, and specialty accelerators such as Google's Edge TPU and NVIDIA's Jetson Nano. This chapter also addresses the trade-offs between performance and power consumption, highlights the specific challenges of this trade-off today, and discusses potential developments in TinyML hardware that could lead to improvements in the future.

candidates.title: Power Management in Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) is transforming intelligent applications by allowing machine learning inference directly on resource-constrained edge devices. Because the majority of TinyML systems will operate in environments with limited battery life or energy harvesting, managing the power of such systems will play a significant role in the success or failure of their intended applications. In this chapter, we provide a detailed account of power management in TinyML systems, starting with the need and challenges presented by power-constrained environments. We explore energy-harvesting methods that allow devices to operate, and we provide strategies for managing and optimizing power consumption. Next, we discuss power profiling at both hardware and software layers, identifying the primary sources of energy usage and suggesting techniques for power-aware profiling. The chapter also focuses on energy-efficient machine learning models (including low-power neural architectures) and energy-aware software tools that decrease total consumption. We discuss the multitude of optimization techniques in hardware, software, operating systems, and hybrid (hardware/software) solutions that improve system lifetime without compromising performance. To show real-world examples of power-efficient TinyML applications, we provide several relevant case studies. Finally, we suggest future research directions and emphasize the need for adaptive, context-aware power management methods. This will provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners developing sustainable design methods for low-power intelligent systems on the edge.

candidates.title: Analysis of Model Compression Techniques for Tiny Machine Learning
candidates.abstract: This chapter explores tiny machine learning (TinyML) as a means to help compress machine learning (ML) models for deployment on memory-constrained hardware. Two case studies provide different approaches to developing efficient and compact models capable of being deployed on the edge. The first case study focused on a specific type of acoustic scene classification (ASC) with a defined subset of the Acoustic Scenes dataset, simplifying the task from multiclass classification to binary classification (i.e., identifying the presence of sound vs. not identifying the presence of sound). In this case study, several models were tested, including bilayered neural networks, linear discriminant analysis, subspace discriminant, linear support vector machines (SVM), and logistic regression. It also demonstrated model compression through feature selection with the minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance (MRMR) algorithm, quantized models, and models optimized with memory-aware Bayesian hyperparameter optimization methods. Results show that models such as linear SVM and logistic regression could achieve model sizes below 30 KB while retaining classification accuracy levels up to 86%. Additionally, doubling the number of features from 25 to 50 improved performance and reduced model size. For example, the Bilayered NN_5 model improved performance accuracy from 31% to 82.67%, and a new model size of even less than 10 KB. The results display the potential for deploying TinyML to support intelligent systems on devices with limited memory resources, such as hearing aids. Image classification is considered with a focus on deploying a deep learning model on embedded platforms like Raspberry Pi, in case study 2. This method uses transfer learning using the CIFAR-10 dataset. The authors use a two-stage compression pipeline consisting of filter pruning based on Taylor-based importance scoring and 8-bit quantization. After the pruning is complete, the authors fine-tune the pruned models to recover performance. The authors also used post-training quantization techniques to reduce the memory requirement and inference time of the model, which could be used at the edge.

candidates.title: Embedded Systems and Internet of Things Foundations
candidates.abstract: The convergence of embedded systems and the Internet of Things (IoT) has accelerated the development of tiny machine learning (TinyML) real-time intelligence, which is delivered on ultra-low-power devices. Thus, this chapter examines the architecture, design methodologies, and emerging roles of embedded systems within the broader IoT ecosystem. This chapter provides a foundational understanding of embedded systems, establishing the components and structures of embedded systems, putting embedded system architectures into the context of IoT architectures, and understanding the increasing roles of embedded systems in improving intelligent edge computing. A detailed examination of embedded architectures, real-time operating systems, and performance limitations provided discourses on the trade-offs designers face between the outcome of embedded systems for real-world applications and the intentional consequences of designs. In the architectural context of IoT, smart services will realise their full potential when they leverage reliable, communicating sensors and actuators included in their design, and direct human intervention at the history collection void. A closer examination of the IoT architecture with its layers opened up communication protocols with embedded sensors and actuators, which are the main drivers combining the edges to connect. Considering the context of embedded IoT, the editors analyzed data processing, secure communication, and deployment to the real world. Based on this discussion of traditional embodied intelligence, the chapter will consider IoT and the challenges of deploying artificial intelligence (AI) as a service, and review the literature in which academic researchers and industry organizations are engaged in deploying TinyML on constrained hardware. A focused discussion follows on how embedded platforms facilitate the execution of machine learning models, with considerations for tools such as TensorFlow Lite Micro. Design methodologies are analyzed and critiqued with a focus on the principles of hardware-software co-design, performance optimization, and real-time processing. A subset of the findings employed in this chapter is based on benchmarking studies and inference-time analysis performed across a wide range of microcontroller platforms. Finally, examples have been provided with an application focus ranging from smart homes, industrial automation, and healthcare to show how the trends are being harnessed. Future directions of the field, namely sustainable edge AI, interoperability, and on-device learning, are provided before concluding. This chapter illustrates that embedded systems and IoT represent the foundation for the next generation of intelligent systems.

candidates.title: Yeah Hand v1.3: an open source tendon-driven robotic and prosthetic hand
candidates.abstract: Open source anthropomorphic hand, 3D-printable, usable as a robotic end effector and as an active prosthetic hand. Successor of Rebelia V1 (OSHWA certified IT000021, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23394100). Five serial bus servomotors housed in the internal skeleton of the hand drive the fingers through antagonistic flexion and extension tendons. Each tendon end runs in its own PTFE Bowden tube, seated in holes, tunnels and slots of the skeleton, to a two-part spool (flexion part and extension part) on the actuator flange. Ring and little fingers are coupled directly on the same spool. The thumb rotation servo, with the thumb base on its flange, is mounted on a removable platform. The ESP32 firmware provides whole-hand calibration, force-limited grasps, grasp presets, a ROS mode streaming position, load, voltage, temperature and current of every actuator, and two-channel FFT-based EMG control in the prosthetic version. Published as open source hardware and as a public technical disclosure (prior art). First published on GitHub on 26 November 2025 as Rebelia V2, i.e. Yeah Hand v1.0 (opsobot/rebelia, branch V2) Hardware: CERN-OHL-S-2.0. Firmware: GPL-3.0-or-later. Documentation and images: CC-BY-SA-4.0. "Yeah Hand" is a registered EU trademark (no. 019374244).

candidates.title: Yeah Hand (formerly Rebelia): an open source tendon-driven robotic and prosthetic hand
candidates.abstract: Open source anthropomorphic hand, fully 3D-printable, usable as a robotic end effector and as an active prosthetic hand. Five serial bus servomotors housed in the internal skeleton of the hand drive the fingers through antagonistic flexion and extension tendons wound in opposite directions on one spool per actuator. Ring and little fingers share one actuator through a sliding tendon loop that lets them adapt to the object. The thumb base is mounted directly on the output flange of the thumb rotation actuator. The ESP32-based firmware performs load-based tendon calibration at start-up, force-limited grasps and grasp presets controlled by a single closure value. In the prosthetic version, two surface EMG channels are processed by FFT and compared with two intensity thresholds to open, close or hold the hand; the grasp can be selected by rotating the unpowered thumb by hand. This record contains the complete design files (CAD, STL, electronic board, firmware) and documentation. It is published as open source hardware and as a public technical disclosure (prior art). First public disclosure on GitHub: 3 March 2025. Hardware: CERN-OHL-S-2.0. Firmware: GPL-3.0-or-later. Documentation and images: CC-BY-SA-4.0. "Yeah Hand" is a registered EU trademark.

candidates.title: Rethinking Robot Ownership: Comparing Public, Corporate, and Private Ownership Models
candidates.abstract: General-purpose robots, or robots that can autonomously and collaboratively perform a wide range of tasks, are almost universally imagined with a private ownership model throughout the robotics research and development process, in which individual households purchase, own, and maintain their own robots. In this paper, we argue that robot ownership should instead be treated as a central socio-technical design choice that fundamentally shapes who benefits from robotics, how robots are deployed, and which research directions become prioritized. We analyze three ownership models for general-purpose robots: private ownership; corporate ownership, in which firms retain ownership and provide access through subscriptions, rentals, or per-task fees; and shared ownership, in which robots function as community resources or public goods accessed through institutions such as libraries, cooperatives, or community centers. We examine how each ownership model structures access to robots and people’s relationships with them along key socio-technical axes including monetization, distribution, repair and maintenance, and liability for harms. We show that the de facto focus on private ownership risks entrenching unequal access to a potentially transformative technology due to its monetary, temporal, and logistical costs. More broadly, we argue that ownership assumptions quietly but powerfully shape robotics research agendas, contributing to hegemonic practices that remain largely invisible in funding, design, and evaluation. We contend that shared ownership is particularly promising for expanding access to robots and improving human–robot interaction, but that realizing this potential requires shifts in both research practices and policy frameworks.

candidates.title: Emotional attachment and problematic involvement with socially interactive AI: A critical narrative review of embodied and conversational systems
candidates.abstract: Background: Socially interactive AI can elicit meaningful relational experiences. Studies often conflate attachment, anthropomorphism, companionship, dependence, and addiction, and group embodied robots with dissimilar software. Methods: This critical narrative review of a reconstructed, non-exhaustive corpus (Grant & Booth, 2009) is interpretive, not aggregative, because the initial search records disagree. We rebuilt the evidence set from the initially identified literature, separated primary from contextual sources, and sorted them by embodiment and dialogue architecture. Coding kept attachment functions distinct from related constructs. A reproducible OpenAlex and PubMed search (2010-2025) retrieved only one of the 12 primary reports. A coverage probe found 34 further provisionally eligible reports. We claim no exhaustive coverage or full PRISMA compliance. Results: Reclassification left 12 primary reports and seven contextual sources. In these reports, relational significance appeared with embodied robots, non-LLM systems, and generative systems, carried by co-presence and touch or by conversational contingency, personalisation, and apparent continuity. Most measured companionship, trust, social presence, perceived support, or one problematic-use indicator. Few covered more than one attachment-system function. None established a behavioural-addiction syndrome. The predominantly cross-sectional, self-selected evidence cannot establish whether heavier use causes loneliness. Conclusions: A relationship with an AI system can matter without amounting to reciprocal human attachment or behavioural addiction. Within the reviewed corpus, the evidence supports a broad, uneven continuum of involvement. Omitted studies may change the apparent mix of constructs, technologies, and outcomes. Progress requires longitudinal, technology-stratified studies with construct-specific measures that establish temporal order and impairment and separate embodiment from generative capability.

candidates.title: Cognitive Ergonomics in Robotics
candidates.abstract: Work tasks performed by humans within any work system are the connecting elements between humans and other system elements such as deployed technologies. Fundamental to any task performance are mental processes of those individuals acting within any socio-technical system. Perception, attention, learning, memory and reasoning are just examples of these processes. Within human factors, they are typically studied to evaluate, for instance, mental workload and situation awareness of technology users, whose errors can dramatically impact the safety and the performance of the system. Accordingly, this chapter presents concepts from cognitive ergonomics. These concepts should be considered within Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) studies and applications in order to assess and improve the design of robots which can interact with humans in terms of technology acceptance, usability, accessibility, and, overall, user experience. This chapter describes different effects on humans related to the interaction with robotic systems. Furthermore, specific HRI design elements and recommendations will be outlined. The chapter closes with an overview on quantitative and qualitative methods proposed to evaluate and to assess different aspects of HRI.

candidates.title: Inspect Robots: Evaluating the Capabilities and Safety of Embodied AI
candidates.abstract: General purpose language models are increasingly able to control robotic hardware. Understanding the capabilities and safety of these models when embodied is therefore increasingly important for understanding their societal impact and risks. To this end, we introduce Inspect Robots, a modular, open-source framework for developing and running evaluations of embodied agents. Inspect Robots pairs customizable, reusable abstractions for specifying physical evaluations and analyzing their results with infrastructure that automates evaluation setup, execution and termination. We demonstrate Inspect Robots by using it to evaluate the capabilities and safety of six policies based on frontier language models. Inspect Robots has seen significant early uptake, receiving nearly 100,000 downloads in the three months since its release.

candidates.title: Building robots
candidates.abstract: Physical robots consist of sensors, actuators, computing components, and structural elements to hold them together. The hardest part of robotics for many newcomers has traditionally been the mounting of these components together to create actual physical robots. There are no widely agreed standards for structures and mounts, so most robots need custom physical components for making them fit together. Luckily, this has recently got a lot easier and cheaper. Improvements have been due to advances in 3D printing and open-source hardware standards. This chapter gives a tour of everything you need to set up your own garage mechatronics lab and mount sensors, actuators and embedded computers together in a robot body.

candidates.title: Robotic Safety as Situated Practice: A Three-Way Innovation Ecosystem
candidates.abstract: Abstract The safe operation of wearable assistive robotic systems in care settings depends on organisational practices as well as device specifications. Health and social care professionals (HSCPs) sustain these practices in organisations, but are typically excluded from robotic innovation processes. This paper introduces a three-way responsible innovation ecosystem approach to address this gap. The ecosystem brings HSCPs, service users and robotics developers into productive relation at multiple points along the innovation lifecycle of a pneumatic wearable device. We employ a two-track methods approach. Engineering characterisation including burst testing of the device; and interpretive co-creation such as focus groups, workshops and formative evaluation. A documented co-creation protocol structures iterative engagement, with interpretive steps between sessions shaping subsequent interactions. We make three contributions. (1) Engineering findings progress safety and acceptance specifications for a soft robotic wearable device, including systematic material characterisation, a review of existing standards (which do not yet address upper-limb soft wearables), and new situated measures of acceptability. (2) Interpretive results show how safety in assistive robotics is collectively accomplished through organisational practices such as training and the development of professional norms and capabilities. These findings challenge approaches that frame safety as a design property or alignment problem. (3) Methodologically we present a full co-creation protocol that demonstrates our responsible innovation ecosystem. The ecosystem approach demonstrates how engineering and interpretive knowledge must combine to support safe deployment of assistive robots in care settings. The study illustrates how safety is a situated organisational practice and not a property encoded in specifications alone.

candidates.title: Talk, Render, Act: Integrating Social Gesture and Digital Face with Synchronized Speech for Conversational Humanoid Robot
candidates.abstract: Expressive humanoid interaction requires speech, facial animation, and body gestures to form a coherent response. However, many full-body humanoid robots produce speech and gestures without a visually expressive face, while talking-face animation and robot gesture generation are typically developed separately. We present Talk, Render, Act (TRABot), an agent-based framework comprising specialized agents for motion-atom construction, dialogue generation, motion planning, and facial animation. First, to produce natural and semantically meaningful gestures, we construct Robot-Ready Semantic Motion Atoms by segmenting long-form, G1-retargeted BEAT2 motion into units with natural gesture boundaries, human-verified communicative functions, and feasible trajectories. Second, to preserve semantic order and coordinate body motion with the spoken response, we introduce a Semantic-Conditioned Compositional Planner. Given an ordered semantic function sequence and an estimated response duration, the planner selects approved atoms to realize the longest feasible action sequence while accounting for transitions and neutral recovery. Finally, we deploy a Streaming Face-Speech-Body Integration system on a physical G1 humanoid, combining streaming dialogue audio, audio-driven facial animation, and semantically planned body motion in a unified real-time interaction loop. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that TRAbot achieves the best overall performance among all compared conditions in terms of naturalness, expressiveness, and multimodal coherence.

candidates.title: On-Device Multimodal Small Language Models for Privacy- Preserving Edge Intelligence Through Quantization Pruning Distillation and Energy-Efficient Inference
candidates.abstract: On-device multimodal small language models are emerging as a practical foundation for privacypreserving edge intelligence, enabling devices to interpret and generate language while processing images, audio, video, sensor streams, and contextual signals without continuous cloud dependence. Their deployment can reduce data exposure, network latency, connectivity costs, and centralized infrastructure demand; however, limited memory, compute capability, battery capacity, thermal headroom, and accelerator support constrain model design and inference. This review examines architectures, compression techniques, privacy mechanisms, and energy-efficient inference strategies for multimodal small language models operating on smartphones, wearables, vehicles, robots, cameras, and embedded Internet of Things platforms. It develops a deploymentcentric taxonomy covering weight, activation, cache, and modality-encoder quantization; structured, unstructured, token, channel, and modality-aware pruning; response, representation, cross-modal, and task-specific knowledge distillation; and hybrid compression pipelines. The review analyzes how these methods affect language quality, visual and acoustic understanding, cross-modal alignment, robustness, fairness, privacy leakage, memory consumption, latency, throughput, energy per inference, and thermal stability. Particular attention is given to local retrieval, adaptive modality selection, speculative decoding, cache management, early exiting, hardware-aware scheduling, and heterogeneous CPU, GPU, neural, and digital-signal processing. The paper also evaluates secure personalization, federated updates, trusted execution, encrypted storage, sensor permission controls, and data-minimizing telemetry. Comparative evidence is organized by device class, workload, compression target, and evaluation objective. The gap analysis identifies limited reproducibility, inconsistent energy measurement, weak lowresource language coverage, underdeveloped multimodal privacy benchmarks, and insufficient study of sustained inference under thermal throttling. It distinguishes theoretical compression savings from measurable device-level efficiency improvements. The review concludes with standardized reporting recommendations and research priorities for compact, private, reliable, and energy-efficient multimodal intelligence at the edge.

candidates.title: Phygital customer experience and the adoption of immersive technologies in hospitality: an exploratory study with a value co-creation perspective
candidates.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore immersive-technology adoption in hospitality through the Phygital Customer Experience (PH-CX) framework. PH-CX extends existing technology acceptance, service-dominant logic, omnichannel and customer-journey perspectives by emphasizing embodied, co-created and human-centered experience across physical, digital and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated interactions. Design/methodology/approach Using Bayesian Networks, the study examines probabilistic dependencies among perceived usefulness, collaborative value, responsive co-creation attitudes and intention to use immersive technologies. Data was collected from 208 participants exposed to an AI-supported immersive hotel journey scenario. The analysis is exploratory and identifies conditional associations rather than causal effects or latent-variable relationships. Findings Adoption intention was conditionally associated with perceived usefulness, collaborative value and responsiveness to service innovation. The findings suggest that immersive-hospitality engagement involves functional, relational and participatory conditions beyond usefulness alone. However, the item-level results are hypothesis-generating and do not demonstrate PH-CX’s incremental predictive superiority over technology acceptance model (TAM) or service-dominant logic. Research limitations/implications The scenario-based, cross-sectional bayesian network (BN) design cannot model latent constructs, measurement error, mediation or causal effects. Future studies should validate PH-CX dimensions and compare TAM, TAM-plus-service-dominant logic (SDL) and PH-CX models using structural equation modeling, longitudinal designs and holdout-sample prediction. Practical implications Hotels can implement PH-CX through phased AI concierge pilots, cross-platform data integration and guest co-creation mechanisms. Relevant metrics include booking conversion, AI resolution rates, cross-channel engagement, co-creation participation and net promoter score (NPS). Ethical implementation requires transparency, opt-in participation, privacy safeguards, accessibility and human escalation options. Social implications Human-centered phygital hospitality requires safeguards against digital exclusion, surveillance and loss of human warmth. Transparency, agency, equity, privacy and non-digital alternatives are essential for inclusive and trustworthy service innovation. Originality/value The study advances PH-CX as a theory-extending framework linking usefulness, co-creation, embodied experience and ethical safeguards in immersive hospitality. It also proposes experience-design orientation as a future research profile and offers a phased implementation framework for responsible phygital service design.

candidates.title: Adapting Character Personalities: Emotional Resonance in the Transition of Comics to Animation
candidates.abstract: Abstract This paper explores how the adaptation of comic characters into animation reshapes personality and enhances emotional resonance. Rather than a simple shift from static panels to moving images, adaptation is treated as a creative process of negotiation between source material and reinvention for new audiences. Grounded in adaptation theory, transmedia storytelling, and semiotics, the study examines two case studies: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018), a Western example of superhero reinvention through multiverse storytelling and stylistic experimentation, and YuYu Hakusho (1992), a manga-to-anime adaptation that deepens shōnen characterisation and emotional engagement. The analysis demonstrates how animation extends character identity through movement, voice, and pacing, while also navigating challenges of localisation and cultural translation. The findings suggest that the sustainability of transmedia franchises depends on deliberate planning that preserves essential identity traits while allowing flexible reinterpretation across platforms and cultures. Key Words: Animation, Adaptation, Localisation, Comics, Semiotics, Emotional Resonance

candidates.title: A Benchmark for Spatially Grounded Gesture Generation
candidates.abstract: Communication in shared space interweaves verbal and non-verbal signals, and pointing gestures anchor language to the environment: "put the cup on that one" is uninterpretable without the gesture that fixes the referent. Yet no common framework exists for evaluating whether generated gestures indicate their intended referent; distributional metrics reward a gesture aimed at the wrong object as long as it looks natural. We introduce a benchmark for spatially grounded gesture generation, comprising ~2K pointing-annotated clips from naturalistic VR dialogue with ground-truth 3D referents, a task in which systems must decide when, how and where to point within conversational speech, and a protocol that separates temporal alignment, spatial grounding and perceived naturalness. We also provide a flow-matching baseline, MM-Conv-Flow. Evaluating it alongside an independent retrieval-based system and captured human motion, we find that geometric grounding can exceed that of human pointing without any gain in perceived naturalness, showing that referential gesture quality must be measured along separate dimensions.

candidates.title: From Algorithms to Empathy: Emotionally Intelligent AI Companions in Elder Mental Health Care - A scoping review
candidates.abstract: Background: The rising mental health crisis among older people, which is caused by loneliness, cognitive loss, and a lack of emotional support, needs new and caring solutions. This systematic literature review looks at how emotional intelligence (EI) can be added to AI- powered virtual companions and how they can help improve mental health outcomes in elder healthcare services. Objective: The study’s goal is to find out how emotionally intelligent technology can improve traditional eldercare by delivering consistent, caring, customized emotional support by looking at existing applications and conceptual frameworks. Methods: A peer-reviewed literature published between 2010 and 2025 in the Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed databases. Studies that talked about emotional intelligence, virtual companions, mental health outcomes, or the design or implementation of eldercare services were included. A PRISMA-guided screening method chose 87 articles in all. The data was organized using the theme to identify common ideas and patterns in how virtual agents are used to help older people’s mental health. Results: The results show that there are five main themes: Emotional Responsiveness, Conceptual Frameworks, Psychological Outcomes, Usability and Acceptance, Ethical/System Integration, and Health System Integration. The results show that virtual companions with emotional intelligence may help older people feel less lonely, improve their mood, and make them more mentally strong. But the current collection of studies is not very complete; it has few real-world examples and no models that work across other cultures. Conclusion: This paper emphasizes the possibility of emotionally intelligent virtual companions as an aid in mental healthcare for the elderly. It underlines the critical demand for standardized conceptual frameworks, interdisciplinary research, and ethical principles to inform future breakthroughs and implementations. Emotionally intelligent AI technology could drastically transform aged care into a more responsive and person-centred service model in the digital era.

candidates.title: The fake friend dilemma: relational trust and the political economy of conversational AI
candidates.abstract: As conversational AI systems become a larger part of the media landscape, they raise questions about whose interests they serve and the risks they may pose to users. These systems do more than provide information: they increasingly offer advice and companionship through interfaces that can appear supportive and socially responsive. A pressing concern is that users may form social or interpersonal relationships with these systems and place relational trust in them, even when the interests shaping interactions do not fully align with their own. The Fake Friend Dilemma (FFD) describes the problem that follows: the same relational trust that makes conversational AI useful can also leave users open to manipulation and exploitation when institutional interests conflict with their own. Drawing on work on trust, AI alignment, dark patterns, and surveillance capitalism, the paper considers how the FFD can manifest through product sales, propaganda and biased information, behavioral nudging, and surveillance. It also considers possible structural and technical mitigation strategies. The FFD is not simply about AI misleading users. The problem it surfaces is that the trust people place in these systems can itself become a resource for institutional actors seeking to influence behavior or extract information. The FFD is therefore as much a problem of media governance and political economy as it is a technological one.

candidates.title: A System Dynamics Approach to Modeling Trust Dynamics in Conversational AI
candidates.abstract: Abstract Trust plays a central role in how users adopt and rely on conversational AI systems. Research shows that trust does not develop linearly or remains stable over time. Although initially it often increases, it can fluctuate, decline, and even collapse over time, even when the AI’s performance remains constant. Because existing approaches often conceptualize trust as a stable outcome or direct response to specific system cues, they struggle to explain these longer-term patterns of change. In this paper, we conceptualize trust in conversational AI as a dynamic self-regulating process shaped by repeated interaction and feedback mechanisms. Using a system dynamics perspective, we propose a conceptual model grounded in the "Limits to Success" archetype and implement it as a computer simulation. By offering a process-oriented and mechanism-based account of trust development, this work advances trust research beyond static approaches and highlights trust calibration as a dynamic, ongoing process with clear design implications.

candidates.title: Do Virtual Faces Lead to Real Purchases? Investigating AI Anthropomorphism & Its Impact on Purchase Intention
candidates.abstract: The research paper focuses on the impact of AI anthropomorphism on purchase intention, with the mediating role of marketing personalization, entertainment value and perceived homophily in the context of AI influencers/models. Brands around the world are adopting AI marketing tools, in which AI influencers/models are a relatively newer domain. The aim of the research is to fill the gap of research done on AI influencers/models in the Pakistani consumer market, discussing its practical implications on the fashion industry in particular. The study involved a sample size of 220 respondents, Pakistani residents aged 16 to 45 years, who had either seen or interacted with AI influencers/models before in any media type, using convenience and snowball sampling technique for data collection, which was then run through SPSS using Process Hayes Mediation Model 4. The results of the mediation analysis represented that the three proposed hypotheses in the study were accepted. The hypotheses were; marketing personalization mediates the positive relationship between AI anthropomorphism and purchase Intention, entertainment value mediates the positive relationship between AI anthropomorphism and purchase intention, and lastly, entertainment value mediates the positive relationship between AI anthropomorphism and purchase intention. The proven hypotheses signify the importance of the practical implications of the research on the Pakistani fashion industry, as big global brands are moving towards and investing in newer technologies like AI marketing tools. candidates.title: Known-Voice Cloning and the Limits of Personality Transfer for Character Design
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in zero-shot voice cloning systems make it possible to reproduce a recognizable voice from a short recording and attach it to arbitrary virtual characters. Prior work suggests that familiar vocal identity can carry over associated personality impressions to new targets such as robots or virtual characters. However, these works have mainly examined familiarity and personalization effects rather than directly testing whether a cloned familiar voice systematically transfers personality impressions to an embodied virtual character. Such transference raises the concern that cloned voices could be used to manipulate people into engaging with virtual characters as capable social actors. Across two studies, we investigated whether personality impressions transfer when a virtual character speaks with the cloned voice of a familiar person. Study 1 examined this question in a real-world university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer familiar to the participating students. Study 2 examined the same question online using voices of social media content creators and members of their communities. Drawing on the concepts of identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction, we show that evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies. Observed effects were selective and did not generalize across traits or study contexts. In the online study in particular, recognizable voice identity cues activated expectations about the speaker but did not reconstruct the broader person impression. Qualitative responses further indicated that judgments were frequently shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together. Our findings moderate common concerns that cloned voices straightforwardly manipulate people into perceiving artificial characters as capable social actors.

candidates.title: CompanionSim: Synthetic Data for Evaluating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Relationships
candidates.abstract: Many people now see AI systems as not just productivity tools but as social companions. Researchers are eager to study the consequences of AI companionship behaviors, such as validation, which evoke trust, empathy, and attachment in human–human interaction. However, human–AI interaction data is limited and unreliable, slowing research progress. We scale small amounts of real-world data by simulating multi-turn human–chatbot dialogue across a range of chatbot behaviors and use cases. We release CompanionSim: a simulation framework with 2,240 simulated human–chatbot conversations representing 16 chatbot behaviors across seven use cases. Human participants annotated the simulated conversations and real-world conversations in two experiments probing perceptions of companionship behaviors. We conducted Study 1 with a U.S. representative sample (N = 628) and Study 2 across the U.S., U.K., India, and Nigeria (N = 3,646). Surprisingly, we find that companionship behaviors reduced likability, humanlikeness, and trust in AI chatbots. These effects were larger in particular subgroups: women and older participants saw companionship chatbots as less likable, humanlike, and trustworthy. We encourage researchers to leverage real-world and synthetic data together to study the differential impacts of AI companions and to create benchmark evaluations of AI chatbots.

candidates.title: Inclusive AI: Rethinking AI-based Multimodal Interaction for Diverse and Underrepresented Users
candidates.abstract: Socially interactive AI systems increasingly shape how people access information, services, and support. However, many of these systems are designed around normative assumptions about communication, behavior, and social interaction, creating barriers for people with disabilities and other underrepresented populations. As a result, social AI technologies risk excluding users whose communicative styles diverge from dominant norms, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, employment, and autonomous systems. This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from HCI, HRI, AI, and related fields to explore the challenges and opportunities of designing inclusive social AI. Discussions will address disability bias, limitations of current datasets and models, methodological challenges in capturing diverse interaction behaviors, and ethical considerations in the development of socially interactive technologies. Through participatory activities, attendees will identify research gaps and future directions. Outcomes include a community-authored white paper, shared resources, and the establishment of a multidisciplinary research network to advance inclusive social AI.

candidates.title: RL-Robotutor: a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for multimodal robot tutoring
candidates.abstract: Personalised robot tutoring requires real-time pedagogical decision-making under uncertain and multimodal learner states. Existing intelligent tutoring and robot-assisted learning systems often rely on static rules, single-modality learner modelling, or short-term correctness-oriented optimisation, which limits their capacity to balance knowledge acquisition, engagement, retention, and safe embodied interaction. RL-Robotutor is presented as a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that integrates cognitive knowledge-tracing signals, facial-expression and gaze-derived affective cues, and behavioural interaction logs through transformer-based fusion. A PPO-trained meta-policy selects among specialised modules for learner assessment, curriculum adaptation, strategy selection, and reflective feedback, while a hybrid reward combines immediate learning performance, engagement, long-term learning gain, and safety. The evidence is reported by source: five public knowledge-tracing datasets assess the cognitive prediction component; controlled simulator experiments assess policy learning, reward ablation, and multimodal fusion; and a randomised robot-tutoring study assesses embodied interaction with 120 undergraduate participants. RL-Robotutor outperforms rule-based, flat reinforcement-learning, knowledge-tracing, and LLM-based comparators. In the human study, the learning gain is 0.62, compared with 0.40 for the rule-based robot condition. The full hybrid reward improves simulator learning gain by 19% over correctness-only optimisation, and full multimodal fusion improves simulator engagement by 17% over text-only modelling. Jetson Orin deployment achieves 48 ms inference latency with an absolute AUC reduction of 0.007, supporting real-time edge execution.
